units.translation: charred by the thunderbolt of Zeus
that a fiery thunderbolt should come from Zeus
he will find a flame stronger than the thunderbolt
that the fire-bearing thunderbolt will come
may the bolt of the thunderbolt check him
may Zeus kill him with a thunderbolt
for the thunderbolt from Zeus is hurled at his eyes
in which the thunderbolt is sealed
and you, having learned nothing, will gain
I shall gain a small escape
but to send what is profitable for the city's victory
it is most profitable for one who is wise not to seem wise
what gain is there for me in living?
do not hold out gain to me and then deprive me
and from this gain another gain is born
for the only gain among the dead
saying that gain comes before later doom
this gain of mine is increased
from these fearful faces I see great gain for these citizens
was the title of a play of Aeschylus
to sting the mind, to mock
to sting the mind, to mock
you mocked me, indeed, as if I were a child

where many copies have Κεγχρείας [Cenchreias]. Scholium: Κέρχνη κρήνη ῎Ἄργους. τὸ ἀπὸ Κέρχνης κατιὸν, ὅ ἐστιν ὄρος [Cenchne is a spring of Argos; that which comes down from Cenchne, which is a mountain]. What is added, καὶ ἡ ἄκρα δὲ ὄρος [and the headland is also a mountain], refers to the beginning of the next verse, where Λέρνης ἄκρην τε [and the headland of Lerna] is written in M, about which will be said under the word Λέρνη [Lerna].
Cenchne is a spring of Argos; that which comes down from Cenchne, which is a mountain
and the headland is also a mountain
the deep-black hiding place of Tartarus
the seats and hiding places of the just land
under the ancient hiding places of the earth
if there is any dark hiding place somewhere
whom not even in death does the earth hide
do not hide within your heart
for the bank hides friendly dispositions
the sides of the bronze cauldron hide the ashes under the enemy earth
I trust that he will cast the head of Zeus's opponent before the gates
In the manuscripts: καὶ δαδάτον, κιγδαδάταν [and dadaton, kigdadatan] and other corruptions.
as the grammarian of Cramer explains: see note on fr. 164.
